name: Girirra
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Mekonnen Hundie [Kumbi]. 2015. The Grammar of Girirra (A Lowland East Cushitic Language of Ethiopia). PhD dissertation, Addis Ababa University. xxvii+367 pp. Open-access AAU ETD,https://etd.aau.edu.et/handle/12345678/16304
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonology, §2.4 Tone, pp. 41-45; transcription note p. 14.
catalog_quote: Tosco (2000:111) also points out that “[…] Highland East Cushitic languages are apparently stress accent languages, while many Lowland East Cushitic languages are tonal accent languages with a simple two term opposition [± high]. The above scholars’ discussionson tone and data on Girirra may help us to group this language, as one of the tonal languages, with two basic tones: high (H) and low (L). Moreover,in Girirra high (H) and low (L) tone is identifiedat the lexical level on nouns and verbs. That is, meaning distinction at lexical levels that is based on the tone variation is identified. However, apart from these lexical items and one instance of tone, that marks interrogative clause (cf.9.5.1.4.),the grammatical function of tone is not identified. [p. 41] ... The high tone is represented by the acute accent (́), while low tone is left unmarked. Tone is revealed only on vowels, there is no tone-bearing consonant. [p. 42] ... 97. HH sóór ‘wasp’ / LL soor ‘porridge’ / H ɗáw ‘hit, strike’ / L ɗaw ‘foot’ / LH baláár ‘shoulder’ / LL balaar ‘wide’ ... To sum up, the data presented in this study seems that Girirra is a tonal language. The assignment of tone in different words, however, is not predicted. [p. 45]

Both halves of the quote are present verbatim, including the compilation-together typos: line 2106-2108 "The above scholars' discussionson tone and data on Girirra may help us to group this language, as one of the tonal languages, with two basic tones: high (H) and low (L). Moreover,in Girirra high (H) and low (L) tone is identifiedat the lexical level on nouns and verbs." sits on PDF page 60 (form-feed count), whose printed folio is 41; lines 2231-2232 "To sum up, the data presented in this study seems that Girirra is a tonal language. The assignment of tone in different words, however, is not predicted." sit on PDF page 64,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No statement on word stress. The only full grammar treats Girirra tentatively as a tone language with two lexical tones (H, L) contrasting on nouns and verbs (minimal pairs such as sóór 'wasp' / soor 'porridge', ɗáw 'hit' / ɗaw 'foot'); tone patterns across mono- to four-syllable words are listed but the author says tone assignment is not predictable and that the tonal/non-tonal status needs instrumental follow-up. The author quotes Tosco 2000 that Lowland East Cushitic languages are 'tonal accent languages with a simple two term opposition [± high]' but makes no stress claim for Girirra. The earlier phonology (Abdurahim 1993: 65) explicitly leaves 'syllable weight, stress assignment etc.' to future study.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone said to have one grammatical use, marking interrogative clauses in the perfective (§9.5.1.4, cf. p. 41); otherwise lexical only. Author hedges: 'labeling Girirra as tonal or non-tonal language requires some further investigation' (p. 14).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated lexical items, nouns and verbs in citation form); texts in the grammar are not tone-marked. Description is impressionistic, no instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: Girirra (giri1245, gii), self-name Girirro/Garirro, language Af-Girirra; spoken around Elkerre/Sarar (Afder Zone, Somali Region; formerly Elkerre Awraja, Bale). Abdurahim 1993:1 says there are no significant dialects; Banti 2010 lists Girirra as a sixth Somali dialect group, Mekonnen 2015 (pp. 5-8) argues it is a separate Lowland East Cushitic language, not mutually intelligible with Somali or Oromo. Mekonnen's data come from the Girirra community itself (no sub-dialect named).

sources.note: Chapter 2 Phonology has no stress section; §2.4 Tone (pp. 41-45) tentatively classifies Girirra as a tone language with lexical H/L on nouns and verbs, tone assignment 'not predicted'; the only occurrence of 'stress' in the Girirra description is a quotation of Tosco 2000 that Highland East Cushitic are stress-accent and Lowland East Cushitic 'tonal accent' languages; p. 14 note: texts not marked for tone because tonal/non-tonal labelling 'requires some further investigation'.

sources.citation: Abdurahim Adem. 1993. The Phonology of Girirra. MA thesis, Addis Ababa University. vii+75 pp.
sources.note: Whole thesis is segmental/syllabic (features, assimilation, syllable, length, spirantization, voicing); no tone, stress or suprasegmental section; the only Girirra-specific mention is in the Summary, p. 65 (p. 79): 'Girirra syllable plays another important role as a proper domain for the application of certain phonological rules, such as, syllable weight stress assignment etc. which are to be studied in the feature [sic: future].' Also p. 1: 'Since Girirra is restricted to a very small area, there seems to be no significant dialects.'

sources.note: A two-page encyclopaedia article on the Girirra people and language (Glottolog listed by Glottolog as a minimal description, med_type a wordlist or less). Whether it carries a line on tonal accent is unknown; Banti writes on Somali tone/accent elsewhere, so a one-sentence remark is possible but unverified. It predates all tone data on Girirra (Mekonnen 2015 is the first and only tone description; Mekonnen states the only earlier linguistic works are Abdurahim 1993 and Askale 1994, both silent on tone).
